_doc: Reference data for /tools/vinyl-decoder.html, consumed by vinyl-decoder.js. Each entry is one documented runout/matrix convention. 'codes' is a list of alias strings the matcher checks against the user's free-text runout input (or, for scope:'sid', the SID field). Aliases made of only non-alphanumeric characters (symbols) are matched as a literal substring anywhere in the text OR via the symbol picker. Aliases starting with 'SEL:' are picker-only — they never match typed text, only an explicit dropdown selection (used for marks with no easy-to-type glyph, e.g. a hand-drawn bird doodle). Every other alias is matched with wildcard-tolerant logic: <=2 alphanumeric characters requires an isolated whole-token match (to avoid matching inside unrelated numbers/words); >2 characters allows fuzzy substring/partial-coverage matching. 'confidence' must be one of: 'well-documented' | 'commonly cited, some disagreement' | 'possible, low confidence' — this is the BASE tier; the matching engine may downgrade it further for a given match (partial coverage, wildcards used, or single-character codes, which are always capped at the lowest tier).

entries.explanation: George Peckham signed his cutting work with playful phrases rather than plain initials — “A Porky Prime Cut” is the classic one, sometimes shortened to just “Porky”, and “Pecko Duck” is a documented variant.
RL etched in the runout is the signature of mastering engineer Bob Ludwig, one of the most credited names in vinyl and CD mastering.
BG (sometimes written with periods as B.G.) marks mastering by Bernie Grundman, founder of Bernie Grundman Mastering.
Plain AZ in the runout credits Allen Zentz Mastering.
entries.caveat: If the AZ has a small bird, flower, or a メ / ❀ symbol right next to it, that specific combination is documented separately as Brian Gardner's mark (he worked at Allen Zentz) — check the symbol picker below if you see anything drawn alongside the letters.

entries.display: AZ with a small bird / flower motif
entries.explanation: Brian Gardner's runout signature at Allen Zentz Mastering paired the AZ initials with a small bird or flower doodle rather than leaving the initials plain.
entries.symbol_label: AZ + small bird/flower doodle (no plain unicode symbol — pick this if you see AZ with a little drawing next to it)

entries.explanation: A standalone bird doodle, or the メ or ❀ character on its own with no AZ nearby, is also documented as Brian Gardner's mark.
The handwritten AT/GP combination marks Atlantic Records mastering work done by George Piros.
The handwritten AT/DK combination marks Atlantic Records mastering work done by Dennis King.
GF in the runout credits Greg Fulginiti's mastering work at Artisan.
The name Wally etched into the runout credits mastering engineer Wally Traugott.
KG in the runout credits mastering engineer Kevin Gray.
SH is commonly attributed to mastering engineer Steve Hoffman.
entries.caveat: This particular attribution is debated in collector circles — treat SH as a lead worth checking further, not a settled fact.

entries.explanation: TJ in the runout credits mastering engineer Ted Jensen.
GK in the runout credits mastering engineer Gilbert Kong.
LH in the runout credits mastering engineer Lee Hulko.
GC in the runout credits mastering engineer Greg Calbi.
TC in the runout credits mastering engineer Tom Coyne.
The name Doug etched into the runout credits mastering engineer Doug Sax.
RKS in the runout credits mastering engineer Ryan Smith.
JN-H in the runout credits mastering engineer Joe Nino-Hernes.
KW in the runout credits mastering engineer Krieg Wunderlich.

On Blue Note releases, a small cursive “P” in the runout — collectors call it “the ear” because of its shape — marks a Plastylite pressing. “9M” is a separate mark also seen on the earliest Blue Note pressings. Rudy Van Gelder's own engineering stamp evolved over the years: it started as a hand-etched “RVG”, moved to a machine-stamped “RVG”, and later became a machine-stamped “Van Gelder”. Blue Note's stereo catalog numbers also get an “8” added in front of the mono 1500/4000-series number, which is a quick way to tell a stereo pressing from the catalog number alone.
entries.caveat: Scoped to Blue Note releases.

entries.result: Also seen on the earliest Blue Note pressings
entries.explanation: 9M appears alongside the Plastylite “ear” mark on some of the earliest Blue Note pressings.
entries.caveat: Scoped to early Blue Note releases; on its own this is a weak signal.

entries.explanation: RVG is Rudy Van Gelder's engineering credit. It started as a hand-etched “RVG”, then became a machine-stamped “RVG”, and later a machine-stamped “Van Gelder” — the exact form is itself a rough dating clue for the pressing era.

entries.result: Rudy Van Gelder engineering stamp (later era)
entries.explanation: The spelled-out, machine-stamped “Van Gelder” is the later evolution of the same engineering credit that started as hand-etched “RVG”.
The number 56 alone in the runout identifies Columbia's Pitman, New Jersey pressing plant.
The number 73 alone in the runout identifies Columbia's Terre Haute, Indiana pressing plant.
The number 25 alone in the runout identifies Columbia's Santa Maria, California pressing plant.
The number 70 alone in the runout identifies RCA's Indianapolis, Indiana pressing plant.
The number 72 alone in the runout identifies the PRC pressing plant in Richmond, Indiana.
The number 24 alone in the runout identifies the Monarch pressing plant.
The number 30 alone in the runout identifies the Plastic Products pressing plant.
The diamond-P-diamond symbol identifies MCA's Pinckneyville pressing plant.
The boxed-G symbol identifies MCA's Gloversville pressing plant.

entries.result: Columbia Records Pressing Plant, Carrollton, GA
entries.explanation: A standalone G or G1 identifies Columbia's Carrollton, Georgia pressing plant.

entries.result: Capitol Records Pressing Plant, Los Angeles
entries.explanation: A six-pointed asterisk-like symbol or a star in the runout identifies Capitol's Los Angeles pressing plant on pre-1964 pressings.
entries.caveat: Scoped to pre-1964 pressings.

entries.category: Columbia hand-etched plant letters (1950s–60s US jazz era)
entries.explanation: A hand-etched H is documented on 1950s–60s US jazz-era Columbia pressings as the mark of the Hollywood, Alden Drive plant.
entries.caveat: Scoped specifically to 1950s–60s US jazz-era Columbia pressings. A single hand-etched letter is easy to confuse with other conventions — treat it as a weak lead outside that scope.

entries.category: Columbia hand-etched plant letters (1950s–60s US jazz era)
entries.explanation: A hand-etched T is documented on 1950s–60s US jazz-era Columbia pressings as the mark of the Terre Haute plant.
entries.caveat: Scoped specifically to 1950s–60s US jazz-era Columbia pressings. A single hand-etched letter is easy to confuse with other conventions — treat it as a weak lead outside that scope.

entries.category: Columbia hand-etched plant letters (1950s–60s US jazz era)
entries.explanation: A hand-etched S is documented on 1950s–60s US jazz-era Columbia pressings as the mark of the Santa Maria plant.
entries.caveat: Scoped specifically to 1950s–60s US jazz-era Columbia pressings. A single hand-etched letter is easy to confuse with other conventions — treat it as a weak lead outside that scope.

entries.explanation: Rainbo Records used an “S-” prefix followed by digits as its matrix number format from 1976 to 2006.
entries.caveat: Rainbo and RTI both used the same 31.7mm/70mm deep-groove label ring from roughly 1979–2020, so ring size alone can't tell them apart — the matrix format is what disambiguates them.

entries.explanation: RTI's plating matrix format is a number, a period, then a digit in parentheses — that parenthetical digit tells you whether the plating went through a 3-step, 2-step, or newer 1-step process (the 1-step process shows up on releases like MoFi's UltraDisc One-Step titles).
entries.caveat: Rainbo and RTI both used the same 31.7mm/70mm deep-groove label ring from roughly 1979–2020, so ring size alone can't tell them apart — the matrix format is what disambiguates them.

entries.explanation: A W or WC plant marking identifies H.V. Waddell pressings from 1976 to 1984.
entries.caveat: The single-letter “W” form is easy to confuse with unrelated letters — treat it as a weak lead on its own.

entries.explanation: An “Alshire” stamp in the runout identifies the Alshire pressing plant, active 1978–1985.
A filled-circle symbol, or the digit 1 on its own, marks Decca's Gloversville, NY pressing plant.
entries.caveat: A lone digit is one of the weakest possible signals — many unrelated numbers in a runout could coincidentally be a 1. Treat this as a weak lead only, especially without the symbol form.

entries.explanation: A filled-diamond symbol, or the digit 2 on its own, marks Decca's Pinckneyville, IL pressing plant.
entries.caveat: A lone digit is one of the weakest possible signals — many unrelated numbers in a runout could coincidentally be a 2. Treat this as a weak lead only, especially without the symbol form.

entries.explanation: A star symbol marks Decca's Los Angeles pressing plant on pressings from 1949 to 1954.
entries.caveat: Scoped to 1949–54 — the same plant used a digit-5 convention in the earlier 1946–49 window instead (a separate entry below).

entries.explanation: The digit 5 on its own marks Decca's Los Angeles pressing plant on pressings from 1946 to 1949.
entries.caveat: Scoped to 1946–49, and a lone digit is one of the weakest possible signals — treat this as a weak lead only.

entries.template: The digits after MPO look like a 2-digit pressing year (“{1}”) followed by a 6-digit stamper number (“{2}”), per MPO's own format.
entries.explanation: MPO's runout format is its logo followed by a 2-digit pressing year and a 6-digit stamper number.
entries.caveat: We don't guess the century from the 2 digits alone — it's just the last two digits of whichever year the disc was pressed.
entries.source: Reddit corpus (worked example against Lana Del Rey's Norman Fucking Rockwell!)

entries.explanation: LT40 is a Mastering SID (IFPI-registered) code identifying Cinram as the facility that mastered the disc.
entries.caveat: A Mastering SID says where it was mastered, not where (or when) it was pressed — that's the separate Mould SID.

entries.explanation: IFPI 6000 is a Mould SID code identifying Cinram as the plant where the disc was physically pressed.
entries.caveat: A Mould SID says where it was pressed, not where it was mastered — that's the separate Mastering SID. Neither SID tells you the release date on its own; a nearby glass-mastering date code (a different string) is not the same thing as the release date.

entries.result: Side marking (A/B side, or side 1/2 of each cut for double LPs)
entries.explanation: A matrix number ending in A or B (or A1/B1, A2/B2 for double LPs) is commonly used to mark which side it belongs to, when the label itself doesn't say.
entries.caveat: This is not reliable. For Direct Metal Mastering (DMM) pressings specifically, a documented case shows “E1/B” meaning “side 1 of a 12″ LP pressed from the 2nd DMM cut” — seeing an A does not necessarily mean you're looking at side A.

entries.result: Possibly first press/mastering, or a new pressing/cut
entries.explanation: A trailing # symbol is sometimes used to flag a first pressing/mastering, or a new pressing/cut.
entries.caveat: Our source hedges this one too (“usually”, not “always”) — treat it as a loose convention, not a rule.
